wanted to try out linux as I thought it would be fun to do and am unsatisfied with windows 10. I am dual booting mint with 10 (because I game on windows), and I have to say I am loving mint! Any tips for a newbie that doesn't know much about the OS? Cool software, shortcuts, etc?
New linux user, chose to try out mint first and love it! Any basic tips for a newbie?

The #1 thing I would suggest for any new linux user (not just mint) is patience. When you encounter things that don't work, or more likely, don't work the way you expect, take your time, read the documentation/message boards/etc. Give yourself time to adjust and learn.

Next, especially for gamers, start looking at what games you can transition over to your linux partition. If you're a Steam user, install the linux Steam client and see what from your library already works natively. Look at tools like wine, playonlinux, crossover, etc to get the rest of them working. You may need to switch which video driver you're using - an opportunity to learn more about your new OS. You'll be surprised how easy gaming on linux is these days.

Beyond that, I'd say "just use it". Use your mint install as often as you can and for as many things as you can. If you find something you (think) you can't do in linux/can only do in windows, spend some time looking into it deeper. There are very, very few things these days that can truly only be done on a single OS.

oh, and of course, sub to all of the relevant subs' here. /linuxmint, /linux, /linuxquestions, /linuxgaming, and for lolz, /linuxmasterrace. :)

Sorry for the delay but that has been a very beneficial thing in the past and makes building files easier. I am pretty sure there's a post on the Linux Mint user forums about it. Either way, Google will show the way. I make use of the forums and the IRC chat once in a while. Sometimes I go to help (which helps me learn) and other times I go to ask questions. It works out well, I think. I also like reading other questions and answers - you can learn a lot that way.

Save your data often - backups are important. You can copy the entire /home directory to an external drive. Then, when things go South you can just install your applications again and copy that data back and have your configurations that you had before. You can also just use something like Acronis. I make it easier on myself and just store stuff over NAS that I have configured just for this reason. I don't worry about saving a profile (though I do want to do network logons and save some more effort - I also make use of VNC quite a bit) a whole lot. I can (and sometimes do) just run off of a Live DVD or thumbdrive.

Get, install, and learn to use "boot-repair." It's handy and easy but it has some powerful options. You could do it with editing GRUB's config file, well most of it - I am pretty sure. It's easier and a nice GUI is handy so I find that to be the easiest choice.

Basically, anything that makes it easier for you to break it is a good thing. The only way you're going to learn (other than as a user) is to break stuff and be forced to fix it. The more you break then the more you'll learn. If there's a button and you do not know what it does? Backup your data and push that. They wouldn't have put a button there if they didn't want you to push it. You might as well figure out what it does.

Anyhow, I saw your old post so I figured I'd chime in. I'm really not kidding about the breaking thing. It helps, a lot, to break stuff. You are then forced to learn. Also, I'd not dual boot. Just use your Linux distro of choice and make the commitment to move away and learn new stuff. It's not as hard as it is made out to be. It has become quite simple over the years. There are lots of resources for help but, most importantly, you have to be able to help yourself and willing to try. When they say RTFM it is probably a good idea to read the manual and then ask any further questions. If you can say, "I've tried this and this but I still have this as a problem and my system state is this with this hardware and I am trying to accomplish this." You'll probably get good information.

It is not bug free and there are problems - even in Mint. There's a bunch of issues that seem to crop up depending on my hardware - I've got way too many computers.
